paras: The Plymouth triple lynching was the killing of three Black prisoners, Matthew Blount, his brother Jack Blount and Patterson Spruill, by masked men at Plymouth, Washington County, North Carolina, around midnight on Thursday, January 26, 1888. Held on a charge of murdering a traveling peddler near Creswell, the men were taken from the jailer, tied to trees about a mile from town and shot to death. The killing was reported nationally by wire, a Raleigh correspondent called it the state's first lynching in many months, and no lyncher was identified.

On January 4 a Raleigh telegram reported that the body of an itinerant clock-mender, named by a letter in his pocket as E. Dawman, had been found in the woods near Cresswell, and that three Black men had been arrested, one of whom confessed to seeing another kill him. Feeling ran high around Creswell, and precautions were taken because a lynching "was expected at any moment," though the Richmond Dispatch's correspondent said vigilance had lately been relaxed and the accused awaited trial at the spring term.

Shortly before midnight masked men, "composed mainly of mounted men" by one Raleigh account, demanded the three prisoners at the jail; according to the wire, the jailer refused but was overpowered. The prisoners were taken to woods outside town and tied to trees, and the wire said they begged for mercy and were allowed only a moment to pray before the lynchers fired "volley after volley."

The bodies were found the next morning still bound to the trees, and the Edenton Fisherman and Farmer heard that the clothes of one were on fire, supposedly from the powder. The wire described Matthew Blount as a preacher "of some local notoriety" who had lost an arm, and a longer version said Spruitt had confessed that "Preacher Blount" did the killing.

On February 2 the Dispatch's Raleigh correspondent reported that no clue to the identity of the mob had been found, though there were rumors the grand jury would act, and that "false rumors" of race trouble at Plymouth had come to nothing. An incendiary fire there on February 1 burned the Episcopal rectory and a hotel; no paper linked it to the lynching. No report of an inquest, an indictment or a trial of the fourth accused man appears in the coverage. Later Raleigh letters counted the three among the state's 1888 lynchings, including "two triple lynchings, one at Plymouth, the other at Oxford."

Most papers took the story from a wire dispatch datelined Plymouth, January 28, printed that day in San Antonio and the next in Indianapolis, Memphis, Fort Worth and St. Paul. Its opening line, "Lynch law ran riot here," cast the event as disorder, yet the same text called the dead men "wretches" and gave the charge against them without qualification. Headlines ranged from "Three Negro Murderers Shot to Death by a Mob" in the Watertown Republican to "Southern Justice" in the Stark County Democrat, whose deck spoke of sending "the Souls of Three Murderers Into Eternity Over the Usual Route." Brief digests garbled the facts, saying the men were "hanged by a mob" or placing the event at "Plymouth, Missouri."

Raleigh correspondents, reprinted in the Charlotte Messenger, gave North Carolina readers the story and treated the dead men's guilt as settled, writing of "the negroes who murdered the peddler." The Asheville Citizen dissented, calling "the Plymouth massacre or lynching" a deed "done in cold blood" and the lynchers "murderers," though it held lynch law excusable for one crime. Months later the Dispatch's correspondent wrote that the three had been "disposed of at Plymouth by his Honor Judge Lynch."

Accounts of the murder differ: Raleigh reports named the dead man E. or Edward Dawman, a clock-mender or jeweler, killed December 23 with blows to the head, while the wire called him John Dawson, a peddler, choked on New Year's day. The first report, which put the body's discovery on January 3 after four or five days, fits neither date, and it and the wire gave three arrests where the Raleigh letters gave four. Names vary (Jack or John Blount; Spruill, Spruitt or Sherwitt), and some reports date the lynching January 27, consistent with a midnight seizure.

The national wire (A5), independent Raleigh letters (A7, A11) and an Edenton report (A25) agree that three named prisoners were taken from the Plymouth jail and shot near town.

accounts.gist: Masked men overpowered the jailer before midnight Thursday, took the three to the woods, refused their pleas, and shot them while they were tied to trees; they were charged with killing peddler John Dawson on New Year's day.

accounts.label: Raleigh correspondents
accounts.gist: A large, mostly mounted mob took the three; they were among four men arrested Christmas day for the December 23 murder of jeweler Ed. Dawman, one of whom confessed; the lynchers were probably from the Creswell section and acted 'quietly and with system.'

accounts.label: Edenton regional paper
accounts.gist: A gang of masked men took the three about midnight Thursday, January 26, and riddled them with bullets a mile from town; lynching had been talked of for some time.

framing.detail: The wire opened 'Lynch law ran riot here' and called the dead men 'wretches'; northern and western papers ran it under headlines such as 'Lynch Law in North Carolina' and 'Three Negro Murderers Shot to Death by a Mob.'
The Stark County Democrat headed the wire 'Southern Justice', with a sardonic deck about the 'Usual Route' into eternity.
The Asheville Citizen called it 'the Plymouth massacre or lynching', a deed 'in cold blood', and said the lynchers should be punished as murderers, while holding lynch law excusable for one crime.

Raleigh correspondents reported it as news, treating the men's guilt as settled ('the negroes who murdered the peddler'), and later counted it with the state's other lynchings, once with the jocular 'his Honor Judge Lynch.'
